blurb: Why AI runs on graphics chips: parallel cores, memory bandwidth, tensor cores and number formats.

cards.title: Two different bets on speed

steps.p: A CPU has a handful of powerful cores with big caches and branch prediction, built to finish one complicated task as fast as possible.
A GPU has thousands of simpler cores that all run the same instruction on different data. Each is slower, but together they do vastly more work per second.

steps.h: Neural nets are the ideal workload
steps.p: Training and running a model is mostly multiplying huge matrices — millions of independent multiply-adds. That is exactly what a GPU is shaped for.

cards.aside: GPUs evolved to shade millions of pixels independently. Matrix math turned out to be the same kind of problem.

cards.q: Which operation accounts for most of the compute in training an LLM?
cards.why: Matrix multiplication. Attention projections and MLP layers are big matrix multiplies (GEMMs). That is why chip vendors quote performance in FLOPs for exactly that operation.

cards.statement: GPUs were originally designed for AI workloads.
cards.why: False. They were built for graphics. NVIDIA's CUDA (2007) opened them to general computing, and the 2012 AlexNet result showed how well they suited deep learning.

cards.title: AlexNet, the 2012 network that kicked off the deep learning boom, was trained on two gaming GPUs.
cards.detail: Alex Krizhevsky used two NVIDIA GTX 580 cards with 3 GB of memory each, splitting the network across them because it did not fit on one. It trained for about a week.

cards.q: On NVIDIA GPUs, threads are scheduled in groups that execute the same instruction together. How many threads are in one of these warps?
cards.why: 32 threads. A warp issues one instruction for all 32 at once. Programs that keep all 32 doing the same thing get full speed.

cards.statement: If threads in the same warp take different branches of an if-statement, the warp slows down.
cards.why: True — branch divergence. The warp runs both paths one after the other, masking off the threads that did not take each branch. This is why GPU code avoids data-dependent branching.

cards.title: The memory wall

steps.p: Registers and on-chip SRAM are tiny and extremely fast. Off-chip HBM holds tens of gigabytes but is far slower to reach.
Each GPU generation has added arithmetic throughput faster than memory bandwidth. Cores increasingly sit idle waiting for data.

steps.h: So kernels are designed around data movement
steps.p: Fast AI code reuses each byte as many times as possible once it is on-chip. FlashAttention and fused kernels exist mainly for this.

cards.aside: A rule of thumb in performance work: moving data costs more than computing on it.

cards.q: HBM, the memory beside every AI accelerator, stands for…
cards.why: High Bandwidth Memory. DRAM dies are stacked vertically and placed right beside the GPU on a shared silicon base, giving a very wide, short connection.

cards.q: Why is generating text for a single user mostly limited by memory bandwidth, not compute?
options: Every weight must be read from memory for each new token but is used for only a couple of operations
cards.why: Low arithmetic intensity. Producing one token reads every weight once and does ~2 FLOPs with it. The cores finish instantly and wait for the next bytes. Speed ≈ bandwidth ÷ model size.

cards.statement: Batching many users' requests together makes text generation more efficient per user.
cards.why: True. Each weight read from memory can then be used for every request in the batch, raising work per byte. This is the core economics of serving LLMs.

cards.title: An NVIDIA H100 can read its 80 GB of memory roughly 40 times per second.
cards.detail: The SXM version has about 3.35 TB/s of HBM3 bandwidth. A model filling that memory can therefore be swept about 40 times a second, which caps single-stream generation at roughly that many tokens per second.

cards.q: On a roofline chart, a kernel sitting to the left of the "ridge point" is…
cards.why: Memory-bound. The roofline plots achievable FLOPs against arithmetic intensity. Left of the ridge, performance rises with intensity because bandwidth is the limit. Right of it, compute is the ceiling.

cards.title: Doing more math with fewer bits

steps.p: Tensor cores multiply small matrix tiles in a single operation, delivering far more FLOPs than ordinary GPU cores.
Each step down in precision — FP32 to BF16 to FP8 to FP4 — roughly doubles peak throughput and halves memory per value.
Scaling factors, careful rounding and higher-precision accumulators let low-bit formats train and serve models with little quality loss.

cards.aside: Much of the headline performance growth between GPU generations comes from newer, smaller number formats.

cards.q: BF16 became the default training format over FP16 mainly because it…
options: Keeps FP32's exponent range, so values rarely overflow or underflow
cards.why: Range over precision. BF16 has the same 8-bit exponent as FP32, just fewer mantissa bits. Gradients that would overflow or vanish in FP16 stay representable, so no loss scaling is needed.

cards.statement: NVIDIA introduced tensor cores with the Volta generation (V100) in 2017.
cards.why: True. The V100 was the first GPU with tensor cores, initially for FP16 matrix math. Later generations added TF32, BF16, INT8, FP8 and FP4 support.

cards.q: In mixed-precision training, why keep a master copy of the weights in FP32?
options: Small updates would round to zero if added directly to low-precision weights
cards.why: Tiny updates disappear. Learning rate × gradient is often far smaller than the weight itself. In BF16, adding it would round away. Accumulating in FP32 preserves those small steps.

cards.title: DeepSeek-V3 was trained largely in FP8, one of the first frontier-scale runs to do so.
cards.detail: Its 2024 report describes FP8 matrix multiplies with fine-grained scaling and higher-precision accumulation. Combined with other efficiencies, it reported about 2.8 million H800 GPU-hours for the final run.

cards.statement: Lower-precision formats only help inference; training always needs 32-bit floats.
cards.why: False. Training has used 16-bit formats for years and FP8 for the largest recent runs. Only certain parts — accumulators, optimizer state, some sensitive layers — stay in higher precision.

cards.title: Wiring GPUs into one machine

steps.p: Eight GPUs share a fast NVLink fabric — about 900 GB/s per GPU on H100 — so they can exchange data almost like shared memory.
Nodes connect over InfiniBand or high-speed Ethernet, an order of magnitude slower than NVLink.
Training constantly runs operations like all-reduce, where every GPU contributes gradients and receives the sum. Network design decides how fast that happens.

cards.aside: In large clusters, the network can cost as much attention — and money — as the GPUs themselves.

cards.q: In data-parallel training, what does the all-reduce step accomplish?
options: Averages gradients across all GPUs so every copy of the model stays identical
cards.why: Synchronizing gradients. Each GPU computes gradients on its own slice of the batch. All-reduce sums them everywhere so all replicas apply the same update.

cards.q: Analysts often say NVIDIA's strongest moat is not its chips but…
options: CUDA and the software ecosystem built on it
cards.why: CUDA. Nearly two decades of libraries (cuDNN, cuBLAS, NCCL), tooling and developer familiarity make switching costly even when rival hardware is competitive.

cards.statement: Google trains its Gemini models mainly on NVIDIA GPUs.
cards.why: False. Google uses its own TPUs, custom accelerators built around large matrix-multiply units and connected in pods. It is one of the few labs largely independent of NVIDIA.

cards.title: A single H100 SXM GPU can draw up to 700 watts — about as much as a microwave.
cards.detail: An 8-GPU server draws over 10 kW. This is why AI data centers are planned around power and cooling, and why newer racks use direct liquid cooling.

cards.title: Estimate GPU memory in your head
cards.body: Weights need parameters × bytes per parameter. A 70B model in BF16 (2 bytes) needs ~140 GB before any KV cache — more than one 80 GB GPU. At 4-bit it needs ~35 GB.
cards.challenge: Work out how much memory an 8B model needs at 16-bit and at 4-bit. (Answers: ~16 GB and ~4 GB.)
